klnj5t: Adjectives that change meaning with “ser” and “estar”
1tdvtfs: You already know that “ser” presents a characteristic and “estar” a state. With some adjectives, changing the verb changes the meaning of the word. “El abuelo es listo” means he is clever; “El abuelo está listo”, that he is ready. “La familia es rica” is about money; “la carne está rica”, about taste.
172tmvh: With “estar”, several of these adjectives take a preposition: “estar orgulloso de”, “estar seguro de”, “estar interesado en”, “estar listo para”. Other adjectives, such as “tranquilo”, “nervioso” or “serio”, don’t change meaning: with “ser” they describe what someone is like in general; with “estar”, how they are today.
n32i76: Ask yourself whether you are talking about what the person or thing is like, or how it is now. If the adjective is in the table, also check which meaning you want.
1dhgkvx: You mean he bores other people: “ser aburrido”.
unys5d: Two pronouns together: order and position
fpz800: When two pronouns appear, the order is fixed: first “se”, then “te” or “os”, then “me” or “nos”, and finally “lo, la, los, las”. In practice: the person pronoun goes before the thing pronoun (“me lo”, “te la”, “nos los”). And “le” or “les” become “se” before “lo, la, los, las”: you don’t say “le lo”, but “se lo”. To make clear who “se” is, add “a” + person: “Se lo damos a la abuela”.
qfgnob: With a conjugated verb, in any tense, both pronouns go in front: “se lo di”, “se lo he dado” (never between “he” and “dado”), “te lo diría”. In the negative imperative they go after “no”: “No se lo digas”. In the affirmative imperative, the infinitive and the gerund they are attached at the end and almost always need a written accent: “dáselo”, “dárselo”, “dándoselo”. With verb phrases you can choose: “se lo voy a dar” or “voy a dárselo”, but never in the middle and never twice.
pgonts: The person (“te”) goes before the thing (“lo”).
1a5rxd6: Collectives and quantities: “la gente dice”, “la mitad votó / votaron”
v1wba0: A collective noun on its own, even if it refers to many people, takes a singular verb: “La gente dice”, “La familia decidió”, “El público aplaudió”. When a collective or a quantity is followed by “de” + plural noun (“la mayoría de los primos”, “la mitad de los invitados”, “un grupo de vecinos”, “el setenta por ciento de los votos”), the verb can be singular or plural: both options are correct, and the plural is very common.
64muh9: If the noun after “de” is singular, the verb is singular: “La mitad de la torta desapareció”. With “cada uno de” + plural, the verb is singular: “Cada uno de los nietos trajo algo”.

1i4d5xm: Two subjects joined with “y” take a plural verb, and the first person takes priority: “Mi hermano y yo llevamos las bebidas” (nosotros). With “tú y él”, in the Americas and parts of Spain “ustedes” is used (“Tú y Facundo traen la torta”); in the rest of Spain, “vosotros” (“traéis”). “Usted y Marta” always go with “ustedes”. If an adjective refers to masculine and feminine nouns, it goes in the masculine plural: “La torta y el vino estaban buenísimos”.
14f6r0m: With “ni… ni” before the verb, the plural is normal: “Ni la abuela ni el tío sabían nada”. And remember that “haber” meaning that something exists never changes: “Había cuarenta personas”, “Hubo tres discursos”, “Va a haber música”. The form “habían cuarenta personas” is heard in many regions, but it is not the educated standard.

2yyt8p: When you attach one or two pronouns to the end of a verb, the word gets longer, but the strong syllable is still the same one in the verb: “da” → “dá-se-lo”, “contando” → “con-tán-do-se-lo”, “preparar” → “pre-pa-rár-se-la”. The pronouns are weak syllables: don’t stress them.
p6jg: That’s why these words carry a written accent: the strong syllable is far from the end. When listening, the strong syllable of the verb tells you the action; the weak syllables at the end tell you to whom and what: “dámelo” (to me), “dáselo” (to him or her), “dánoslo” (to us).
